name: Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images
description: Paper describing the tiny images dataset and the labeled CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 subsets, including collection from the web, preprocessing, labeling, and use for object recognition experiments.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
rai:dataCollection: The tiny images dataset was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet, using several search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista, and keeping roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. After collecting images for a search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white. The paper also describes collecting labeled subsets by paying students to label images, producing CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data are web images found by searching for every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet, using search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista. The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, though this is described as extremely unreliable.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: over the span of six months
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collecting images for a search term, perfect duplicates were removed and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed. For the labeled subset, duplicates were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like. The dataset was then divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly selected 5000 images from each class.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32 x 32. The paper applies a whitening transformation to decorrelate pixel values and set variance in each dimension to 1. In some experiments, the 1000 least significant principal components were deleted by setting corresponding entries of the diagonal matrix D to zero. Some experiments used 8 x 8 patches from the 32 x 32 images, plus an 8 x 8 subsampled version of the entire image.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with search terms that were hyponyms of the main search term in WordNet. Labelers were instructed to reject images that did not belong to the assigned class. Criteria included that the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?', the image should be photo-realistic, should contain only one prominent instance of the object, and could be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as identity was still clear. Every submitted label was personally verified by the authors.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The search-term label was treated as noisy and labelers were used to filter out mislabeled images. Every submitted label was personally verified by the authors.
rai:dataBiases: The rough labels derived from web search terms are described as extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. The paper also notes properties of the images such as symmetry likely caused by the way people take photographs, making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object.
rai:dataLimitations: The tiny images dataset has no reliable class labels, which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments. The rough labels from search terms are extremely unreliable. The paper also notes that whitening may exaggerate the significance of some directions corresponding mainly to noise.
rai:dataUseCases: Used for unsupervised training of deep generative models on millions of unlabeled tiny color images, and for object recognition experiments using the labeled CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 subsets. The paper divides CIFAR-10 into training and test sets, with 5000 training images per class.
